title: The Composer They Called 'the Skinny Dwarf' Wrote an Opera About One
standfirst: In February 1900 Alma Schindler wrote off Alexander von Zemlinsky for his looks. Twenty-two years later he put a court dwarf destroyed by exactly that verdict on an opera stage. In between, in July 1908, he sat for this portrait — weeks before the painter ran off with Zemlinsky's own sister, and months before the painter was dead.

sections.heading: Alma Schindler Wrote Him Off, and He Never Quite Let Go
sections.body: In February 1900, at a Viennese dinner party, Alma Schindler noted in her diary that the man she had just met was 'dreadfully ugly, almost chinless.' The man was Alexander von Zemlinsky, already conducting at the Carltheater and, within weeks, giving her composition lessons. They became lovers. Zemlinsky stood 157 centimetres to Schindler's 172; her circle nicknamed him ['the skinny dwarf'](https://laopera.org/discover/la-opera-content/new-blog-post-55), and pressed her to end things, citing both his looks and his lack of an international name. On 12 December she wrote to break it off — 'You know how very much I loved you. You have fulfilled me completely. Just as suddenly as this love arrived, it has departed' — and within weeks had taken up with Gustav Mahler, whom she married in 1902. Zemlinsky's reply was a piece of music rather than a letter: [Die Seejungfrau](https://interlude.hk/the-mermaid-and-the-prince/), The Mermaid, completed in 1903 and first performed in 1905, in which he cast himself as the creature who loses the prince to somebody else. He was thirty-six, seven years into that verdict, when he sat for this canvas in the summer of 1908.

sections.heading: A Tall, Narrow Canvas With the Wrong Year on Its Own Label
sections.body: Gerstl painted this in Gmunden, on the Traunsee in Upper Austria, where the Schoenberg circle spent its summers and where he had become embedded enough in the household to be giving Arnold Schoenberg informal painting lessons. The canvas is oil on canvas, 170 by 74 centimetres — tall and narrow, an unusual shape for a single sitter — signed, and inscribed on the back with Gerstl's own Vienna address, [Nußdorferstraße 35](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Richard_Gerstl_-_Alexander_Zemlinsky,_1908.jpg), in the ninth district. The museum dates it to July 1908; WikiArt's own listing gives the same picture as 1907, a year's difference that matters more than it looks, given what happened in the twelve months either side of it. The [Kallir Research Institute](https://www.kallirresearch.org/artists/richard-gerstl/biography/), which did more than any other institution to recover Gerstl's reputation after his death, describes his brushwork as reaching past Austrian and German Expressionism altogether, toward something closer to what American critics would not coin a name for until the 1940s. He is filed as an Expressionist because a corpus has to file him as something. He never lived to hear the word applied to him.

sections.heading: Weeks Later, the Painter Was Sleeping With His Sister
sections.body: The woman at the centre of what came next was Zemlinsky's own sister. Mathilde had [married Arnold Schoenberg in 1901](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Arnold-Schoenberg); their daughter Gertrud, [born the following year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gertrud_Schoenberg), was the eldest of their children. By the summer of 1908, Mathilde and Gerstl — the man who had just spent part of that same holiday painting her brother on the shore of the Traunsee — had grown extremely close. That August she left her husband and children and went with him to Vienna. Friends eventually brought her back in October. Gerstl did not recover. On the night of 4 November 1908 he burned every letter and paper he could find in his studio, hanged himself in front of the mirror, and stabbed himself as well. He was twenty-five. His brother Alois kept what survived — [fewer than a hundred canvases and drawings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Gerstl) — until the dealer Otto Kallir found them around 1930 and gave Gerstl the exhibition, and the reputation, that nobody had given him alive.

sections.heading: A String Quartet the Scholars Still Argue About
sections.body: Arnold Schoenberg was writing his Second String Quartet through exactly this crisis, and dedicated it, in the score itself, 'to my wife.' The last two movements set poems by Stefan George — 'Litanei' and 'Entrückung,' [the latter opening](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_Quartets_%28Schoenberg%29) with a line usually translated as a breath blowing in from other planets — and the quartet's own second movement quotes the Viennese folk tune 'O du lieber Augustin,' a joke folded into music written while his marriage was coming apart. Whether any of that is really about Mathilde and Gerstl is not settled. Peter Jost, writing for the [score's publisher](https://blog.henle.de/en/2022/04/25/a-milestone-in-music-history-schoenbergs-2nd-string-quartet-op-10/), argues the choice of poems is unlikely to be pure coincidence with what Schoenberg's household was living through that summer. The musicologist Steven Cahn, citing research by Ethan Haimo and Raymond Coffer, has disputed this in the same publisher's comments, arguing the composition timeline does not support reading the quartet as a direct response to the affair. Zemlinsky, present for his own family's collapse and absent from the finished score, gets no vote in either reading.

sections.heading: Fourteen Years Later, He Wrote the Dwarf's Opera
sections.body: Zemlinsky did eventually put the nickname on a stage. In 1922 he wrote [Der Zwerg](https://laopera.org/discover/la-opera-content/new-blog-post-55), The Dwarf, based on Oscar Wilde's The Birthday of the Infanta — a story LA Opera's own programme notes trace directly back to Alma Schindler's rejection two decades earlier. By then he had built the career the Schindler family had once found insufficient: first Kapellmeister of the Vienna Volksoper from 1906, then, from 1911 to 1927, conductor at the German theatre in [Prague, where in 1924 he gave the premiere of Schoenberg's Erwartung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_von_Zemlinsky). He fled Vienna as the Nazis closed in during 1933, escaped to New York in 1938, and died in Larchmont in 1942. This canvas, painted on the Traunsee that July, sits right at the hinge: made months before the man who painted it was dead, and years before the composer sitting for it turned his oldest wound into an opera nobody could mistake for anything else.
